core_idea: To take something is to get hold of it and then move it, remove it, use it, or have it, and the other senses grow from these ideas of getting and having.

senses.definition: carry something or go with someone from one place to another place

examples.text: Take an umbrella with you; it might rain.
I'll take the kids to school this morning.
Omar took his mother some soup when she was sick.
We're taking the kids swimming on Saturday.

items: take the dog for a walk

compare.note: bring means carry or lead toward the speaker or the place being talked about; take means away from it
carry says only that you hold something as you move; take says where it goes
fetch means go and get something and come back with it

subsenses.definition: help someone understand something by explaining each step of it

examples.text: Let me take you through the plan one more time.
The nurse took us through the instructions carefully.

items: take someone step by step through something

adaptation.grammar: Take is movement away from the speaker or listener; bring is movement toward them. Many languages have one verb for both directions, or choose the verb by whether the thing is carried or led. Choose take when the movement goes away from where the speaker or listener is.

senses.definition: get hold of something with your hand and lift it or move it toward you

examples.text: She took my hand and smiled.
Take a cookie; there are plenty.
He took the phone from her and hung up.
The nurse took the child by the hand and led him inside.

synonyms.note: for lifting something from a surface

compare.note: you take something and then hold it

subsenses.definition: be already used, owned, or promised to someone, so that no one else can have it

examples.text: Is this seat taken?
Sorry, that name is already taken.
I'd ask her out, but I think she's taken.

senses.definition: remove something from a place, or get something that belongs to someone else without asking

examples.text: Take the batteries out of the toy before you clean it.
Someone took my bag while I was in the pool.
The doctor took a small piece of skin for testing.
Please take your name off the list if you can't come.

synonyms.note: steal says clearly that it was a crime; take is the plain everyday word

compare.note: the phrasal verb for subtracting, mainly British

examples.text: If you take six from ten, you get four.
What do you get if you take three from nine?

adaptation.semantic: Take for stealing is the plain, slightly softer word: someone took my bike. Most languages would say steal here; keep the softness if the language allows it. The remove use (take the batteries out) is often a phrasal or prefixed verb in other languages.

senses.definition: need a particular amount of time, effort, money, or skill in order to be done

examples.text: The drive to the coast takes about two hours.
It took me a week to read the whole book.
examples.note: it takes someone time to do something

examples.text: It takes courage to say no to your boss.
It takes three people to lift that table.

items: it takes an hour to do something

adaptation.grammar: The thing that needs the time is the subject (the trip takes an hour), or it is used: it takes an hour to get there. The person, if mentioned, is an object after take: it took me an hour. There is no passive.

senses.definition: do the action named by the noun that follows, such as a walk, a look, a shower, or a break
senses.explanation: Take carries little meaning of its own here; the noun says what is done. Which nouns go with take is fixed by habit: you take a walk, a shower, a break, or a test, but you make a decision (or, in British English, take one) and have a meal.

examples.text: Let's take a short break and come back at three.
I usually take a shower before breakfast.
Take a look at this photo.
Take a deep breath and try again.

compare.note: British English often has a shower, a bath, a look, or a rest where American English takes one
make a decision, make an effort, make a phone call

subsenses.definition: study a subject at school or college, or do a test or an exam

examples.text: I'm taking chemistry this year.
She took the driving test twice before she passed.
Which classes are you taking next semester?

adaptation.semantic: Every language has its own light verbs: where English takes a shower, a walk, or a break, other languages make, do, give, or have them. Learn each noun with its verb as one unit; the verb cannot be predicted from the meaning.

senses.definition: swallow medicine or a drug, or eat or drink something

examples.text: Take two of these pills after every meal.
Have you taken your medicine today?
Do you take milk in your coffee?
He started taking drugs when he was a teenager.

items: take something three times a day

adaptation.semantic: In many languages the same verb covers eating, drinking, and having a meal (take a coffee, take breakfast). In English you take medicine, drugs, and milk or sugar in a drink, but you have or drink a coffee and have or eat breakfast. I'll take a coffee is only for ordering.

senses.definition: travel by a particular bus, train, taxi, or plane, or go along a particular road or route

examples.text: I take the bus to work most days.
Let's take a taxi; it's raining.
Take the second left after the bridge.
We took the highway to save time.

compare.note: catch a bus means get on it in time; take a bus means travel by it
American English also rides the bus or the train

adaptation.grammar: The vehicle is a direct object with no preposition: take the bus, not take with the bus (though go by bus is correct). Streets and turns are objects too: take the second street on the left.

senses.definition: accept something that is offered or given, or agree to do a job or a duty

examples.text: I've decided to take the job.
They don't take credit cards, so bring cash.
You should take her advice.
Somebody has to take responsibility for the mistake.

items: take the opportunity to do something

subsenses.definition: choose to buy or have something that is offered, for example in a store or a restaurant

examples.text: I'll take the blue one, please.
We'll take a table by the window.
I'll take a large coffee to go.
They took a small apartment near the station for the summer.

senses.definition: find out and write down a measurement, or write down what someone says

examples.text: The nurse took my temperature and blood pressure.
Can I take your name and phone number?
Mari took notes during the lecture.
Could you take a message? Lee isn't here right now.

subsenses.definition: make a photograph or a video of someone or something with a camera

examples.text: Would you take a picture of us?
I took some great photos of the sunset.
She's taking a video of the whole show.

adaptation.semantic: Many languages make or shoot a photograph; English takes one, and the person or thing in the picture follows of. The measuring uses (take someone's temperature, take a reading) translate with measure or record in most languages.

senses.definition: deal with bad news or hard treatment in a particular way, or be able to accept it without being upset

examples.text: She took the news better than we expected.
He can't take a joke.
I can't take this noise anymore!
Ana took it hard when her dog died.

items: can't take much more of something

synonyms.note: for the use with can't: can't stand the noise

adaptation.semantic: This sense often needs two verbs in other languages: react or receive (take the news well) and bear, stand, or put up with (can't take the noise). The adverb well, badly, or hard is almost always present in the first use.

senses.definition: understand or consider something in a particular way

patterns: verb + object + as + noun or adjective

examples.text: I took his silence as a no.
examples.pattern: verb + object + as + noun or adjective

examples.text: Don't take this the wrong way, but that color doesn't suit you.
You should take her warning seriously.
What did you take that comment to mean?

subsenses.definition: believe, often wrongly, that someone or something is a particular kind of person or thing

examples.text: What do you take me for, a fool?
Sorry, I took you for someone else.
I took the man at the door to be the owner.

items: What do you take me for?

subsenses.definition: have a particular opinion about something, or deal with it in a particular way

examples.text: The company takes a strict line on lateness.
Many people take the view that the law should change.
We need to take a different approach to the problem.

adaptation.semantic: Interpret (take something as a joke), mistake (take you for someone else), and adopt (take a position) are separate verbs in many languages. The pattern take something as a noun or adjective is the most common and the hardest to translate word for word.

senses.definition: get control of a place or a person by force, or win something in a competition

examples.text: The army took the city after three days of fighting.
The soldiers took several prisoners.
Yuki took first place in the school competition.
She took the lead early in the race and never lost it.

senses.definition: have enough room for a number of people or things, or need a particular size, kind of fuel, or kind of battery

examples.text: The car takes five people comfortably.
This camera takes ordinary batteries.
What size shoes do you take?
The hall can take two hundred people.

compare.note: hold says how much fits inside; take says what a thing can accept or is made for

adaptation.grammar: No passive and no continuous form: the car takes five people, never is being taken. The object names the number, size, or kind of thing that fits or is needed. For clothes and shoes, American English more often says wear a size.

senses.definition: (of a verb, a noun, or a preposition) be used together with a particular form of another word, such as an object or a plural

examples.text: The verb give can take two objects.
Which preposition does depend take?
Nouns such as furniture do not take a plural.

phrases.definition: relax and not work too hard, or stay calm
phrases.explanation: Also said as a friendly goodbye, and as advice to someone who is angry or worried.

examples.text: The doctor told him to take it easy for a few days.
Take it easy, we've still got plenty of time.
See you tomorrow, take it easy!

phrases.definition: accept exactly what is offered, or get nothing, because the offer will not change
phrases.explanation: Said when making an offer that will not be changed. A person who can take something or leave it does not care much about it: Chocolate? I can take it or leave it.

examples.text: That's my final price: take it or leave it.
The company made us a take-it-or-leave-it offer.

phrases.definition: believe what I say, because I know it from my own experience

examples.text: Take it from me, that road is much slower in the evening.
You'll be glad you went, take it from me.

phrases.definition: expect something to be true or to continue, without thinking about it or being thankful for it
phrases.explanation: Take someone for granted means fail to show that you value a person because you are used to their help.

examples.text: We take clean water for granted until the supply fails.
I took it for granted that the store would be open.
Her family takes her for granted.

adaptation.grammar: With a that-clause, English fills the object slot with it: take it for granted that the store is open. The clause cannot follow granted directly.

phrases.text: take it upon yourself to do something
phrases.definition: decide to do something without being asked, or without having the right to do it

examples.text: Kim took it upon herself to reorganize the whole office.
Nobody asked him to speak; he just took it upon himself.

phrases.definition: accept unfair treatment without protesting or fighting back
phrases.explanation: Almost always used in the negative.

examples.text: We won't take this decision lying down.
She's not the kind of person who takes an insult lying down.

phrases.definition: suppose that something is true because of what you see or know
phrases.explanation: Used to check what you believe is the case, usually with I as the subject; that is often left out.

examples.text: I take it you two have already met.
I take it that the meeting is off?

phrases.text: be taken with someone or something
phrases.definition: like or admire someone or something very much, especially when you first meet them

examples.text: Lee was quite taken with the little house by the lake.
The children were very taken with the new puppy.

phrases.definition: deal with events as they happen, without planning or worrying about what comes next

examples.text: I don't have a plan for the trip; I'll just take it as it comes.
Since her illness, she takes each day as it comes.
examples.note: with each day instead of it

phrases.definition: continue from that point, deciding what to do next when you reach it

examples.text: Let's meet at the station and take it from there.
Fix the first problem, and we'll take it from there.

word_family.note: a take in filming, or someone's view of something
mainly British: the money a business receives

synonym_discrimination.note: Bring means move something toward the speaker or the place being talked about: Bring your photos when you come. Take means move it away or to somewhere else: Take your photos when you go. Carry says only that you hold something while you move and says nothing about direction: She carried the box upstairs. Fetch means go somewhere, get something, and come back with it: Fetch a chair from the kitchen.

usage_note: British English often uses have where American English uses take: have a shower, have a bath, have a look, have a rest. Both varieties take a photo, take a break, and take a walk. For exams, British speakers sit or take them; Americans take them.

learner_errors.incorrect: I took a coffee with Ana after class.
learner_errors.correct: I had a coffee with Ana after class.
learner_errors.note: Take is for medicine, drugs, and milk or sugar in a drink; for drinking or eating something, use have, drink, or eat.

learner_errors.incorrect: It took me long time to find it.
learner_errors.correct: It took me a long time to find it.
learner_errors.note: Time is countable in a long time and a short time, so the article is needed.

learner_errors.incorrect: Can you take a photo to me?
learner_errors.correct: Can you take a photo of me?
learner_errors.note: The person or thing in the photo follows of; to would mean that the photo is given to the person.

adaptation.semantic: Take is a very general verb of getting and moving; most languages divide it among several verbs: carry away, lead away, accept, grab, swallow, use a bus, need time, make a photo. Translate by sense, and check the light-verb uses (take a walk, a shower, a photo) one by one.
adaptation.grammar: Take is irregular: take, took, taken. It is almost always transitive: something or someone follows it. The time sense uses it as a subject: it takes an hour to get there. For a vehicle the object is direct: take the bus, not take with the bus.
adaptation.pronunciation: The vowel is the long a of name and cake, so take rhymes with make. The past tense took has the short vowel of book and good, not the vowel of food.
